svg.text: One sentence in. One floor out.
How human intent becomes something a computer can run, and why it loses meaning on the way.
Faster for whom: phone or desktop?
Many meanings live in one sentence.
Shannon measured English at 0.6 to 1.3 bits per letter.
The letters are predictable. The meaning is not.
Fan out to 626 ways of writing it. Re-converge.
LOST: names, style, the author’s reasons
one graph the compiler can reason about
LOST: types become sizes, loops become jumps
Most guesses are right. Bugs live in the rest.
So code bends toward those shapes.
Stop losing meaning at every boundary.
Pick the one that costs least.
Sources: Shannon, “Prediction and Entropy of Printed English,” Bell System Technical Journal, 1951. Lopes et al., “DéjàVu: A Map of Code Duplicates on GitHub,” OOPSLA 2017.
626 languages: an unpublished survey by the OpenIE authors. Python and C results are language spec behavior. C signed overflow is undefined behavior.
